testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States, Part 33
testimony.committee: Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs, United States Senate
testimony.subject: Conditions on Yuma Reservation including education, employment, land leases, relief work, roads, and reimbursement
testimony.key_claims: Nejo represents 435 of approximately 800 Yuma Indians in the Yuma Indian Federation auxiliary. He complained about: (1) Absence of Commissioner Collier from the hearing despite alleged commitment to attend; (2) Land abuses since treaties of 1851-1852; (3) Government schools failing to educate Indians, preferring public schools and higher education including college and university; (4) Attended Carlisle himself; (5) Relief work insufficient, with very young (14-15) and very old (60-100) Indians working while able-bodied men with families have no work; (6) Federation members specifically deprived of work—Owen McKinley lost work after sending delegation to Washington; (7) Albert Snow's 20 acres (10 his, 10 wife's) leased in 1923-1924 for $150, money sent to Los Angeles government office and never received by Snow; (8) Snow received only 50 cents per year for telephone poles on his land; (9) Roads on Yuma Reservation in terrible condition; (10) Martin Domingo's 10-acre allotment had 7 acres taken by Southern Pacific Railroad and Highway 80 with no compensation; (11) Government-built house given to him but empty with no implements or horses to farm with; (12) Educated Indians on reservation unable to use their education because not employed as teachers or in other roles.
testimony.questioner: Senator Burton K. Wheeler; Senator Elmer Thomas

testimony.witness_title: Research Assistant (dollar-a-year), faculty at Johns Hopkins University
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States, Part 33
testimony.committee: Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs, United States Senate
testimony.subject: Conditions at Yuma Reservation, status of Wheeler-Howard bill vote, character of witnesses, leasing records
testimony.key_claims: Gates stated: (1) He is on faculty at Johns Hopkins and was asked by Collier to come to Yuma 3 months prior as a research assistant; (2) Richard Nejo is not a Yuma Indian and has no land in Yuma; (3) He spent 6 weeks doing intensive agronomic survey of Yuma Reservation including inheritance records, allottee representatives, leasing records; (4) Lease money is placed to individual Indians' personal credit accounts, not general funds; (5) John Curran claimed 271 Yuma Indians but did not respond when Gates asked him to verify names; (6) Tribal convention held, 252 of 341 adult Indians (74%) signed petition supporting Wheeler-Howard bill; approximately 70 opposed; (7) Regarding Anna Hollingshead—she visited Gates at his hotel in Yuma multiple times, dresses well, was in a mental sanitarium, is not right in her mind, and Mr. Jolley has given her work; (8) Indians of Yuma making progress and finding their voice through Collier's New Deal; (9) He visited Taos to study housing plans; (10) Board of directors of Collier's Indian defense society.
testimony.questioner: Senator Burton K. Wheeler; Senator Elmer Thomas

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States, Part 33

testimony.subject: Mistreatment of her daughter Anna Hollingshead by agent Jolley
testimony.key_claims: Lewis testified that her daughter Anna Hollingshead has been ill treated by agent Jolley. Anna's husband left 4 years ago; Anna is in ill health with a nervous breakdown. She asked Jolley for work and was only given temporary jobs. When Anna works, Jolley does not provide rations. Anna's oldest boy (16) was taken out of school to work for $21 per month for 10 days per month to support the family of four. Anna's 10-acre allotment land is neglected, full of Johnson grass, diked up, and flooded.

States tribal council was legitimately formed by Indians themselves. Disputes Curran's claim of 400 signatures saying only 341 adults exist on reservation. Claims he got Commissioner out of bed in Washington to telephone about Cocopah killing.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Daughter's illness and lack of proper help
testimony.key_claims: Daughter suffered nervous breakdown and is in hospital for 4 weeks. Daughter was not being helped the right way. Daughter previously worked at lettuce packing in Yuma City after failing to find work at Indian school. Mrs. Lewis is caring for her daughter's children. Daughter currently in Fort Yuma Hospital sanitarium.

testimony.witness_title: Fort Yuma Reservation farmer, Mission Indian Federation member
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Wheeler-Howard bill opposition, tribal council legitimacy, meat sales by policeman, lease money not received, All-American Canal, Cocopah removal
testimony.key_claims: Has lived at Fort Yuma Reservation all his life, farms 23 acres of irrigated land raising alfalfa, has 4 children. Mission Indian Federation has over 500 members and has been organized for 14 years. Opposes Wheeler-Howard bill because wants state law governance. Current tribal council is illegitimate - president appoints council rather than people electing them. Constitution was published in Yuma Sentinel before adoption meeting was held. Policeman Magill sold meat intended for old Indians, Curran bought twice for 25 and 50 cents. Anna Smith lost land she held for 4 years and received no lease money. Wants to know if Indians will be compensated for All-American Canal crossing reservation. Petition with over 400 signatures to remove Superintendent Jolley pending in Washington. Cocopahs being improperly removed from reservation by Jolley.

testimony.witness_title: Non-Indian rancher, graduate of Howard Medical College
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Medical treatment of Cervel baby, gas and meat sales by police, discrimination against Deering
testimony.key_claims: Has lived on Yuma Reservation since 1929, settled on what he thought was Government land now determined to be reservation land. Baby of Mr. and Mrs. Cervel recovered after being taken to Dr. Stacy. Corroborates meat sales allegations. Police also selling gas from reservation. Individuals Hodges and Ben Decours purchased gas from police. Claims he has been discriminated against by prosecution and rejection from Government lands while whites and others are not prosecuted. Cannot personally buy gas because they are too smart to sell to him.

testimony.witness_title: Committee Member, Yuma Indian Federation; Cocopah Tribe
testimony.hearing: Senate Committee on Indian Affairs hearing at Yuma Indian Reservation
testimony.subject: Conditions on Yuma Indian Reservation; Superintendent Jolley; large landowner Billy Poor (self-identified)
testimony.key_claims: Superintendent Jolley refused to give orders to Billy Poor and failed to protect Indians. Federation officials met with Jolley for about one and a half hours. Jolley's men fought against them. Demanded Jolley show authority. Demanded Jolley be removed. Statement made on behalf of Cocopah Tribe and Yuma Indian Federation.

testimony.hearing: Senate Committee on Indian Affairs hearing at Yuma Indian Reservation
testimony.subject: Highway accidents, railroad deaths, allotment abuses, white squatters, relief work discrimination, self-government bill opposition, request for special attorney
testimony.key_claims: Multiple Indians killed or injured on U.S. Highway 80 with no compensation or suits filed by Superintendent Jolley. Railroad killed Indians with no compensation. Allotment no. 639 improperly managed; E. I. Rhodes living on deceased Indian's land. Whites living on Indian land without paying taxes including Jim Parker. White foreman E. A. Breech appointed to irrigation foreman position that should go to an Indian. Superintendent backed discrimination in relief work. Relief work crews excluding Federation Indians. John Collier visited secretly in 1932 and held small meetings. Opposed self-government bill no. 7902 and S. 2755. District attorney never helped Indians. Requested special attorney under contract approved by Secretary of Interior. Indians have Indian judges and policemen for past 14 years.

testimony.hearing: Senate Committee on Indian Affairs hearing
testimony.subject: Land lease abuses, water charges, Winterhaven townsite, relief work problems, railroad deaths, meat rationing abuses, Southern Sierras power poles, Cocopah ejections, Highway 80 compensation, farmer agent failures, reimbursable homes
testimony.key_claims: Mr. Alberts land of 20 acres leased in 1923-24 for $150 with money never given to owners; went to pay water charges. Agent collecting $3 for water charges despite 1903 order setting rate at $2.50. Boy had more than half of 10-acre allotment taken by Southern Pacific, Highway 80, Bard Road, and Spillway without compensation. Winterhaven section taken up by whites, subdivided and sold by McOoon; saloons open on reservation. Relief work very poor; $14,000 appropriation lasted only 3 months; old people aged 60-100 put to work; Federation members refused work. Choice ration meat being sold at 8 cents per pound; worst meat given to old people. Gravel pits leased at exorbitant prices. Roads in terrible condition. Gas stations re-leased or subleased. Cotton gin inactive 4 years but operator still living there. Cocopahs forcibly ejected. 19 flood damage cases never compensated. Southern Sierras power poles through Albert Snow's allotment paying only $1.69/year. Farmer agent never seen in whole year; does not encourage farming. 6 Indians killed by railroad total under Jolley and Odle. Reimbursable homes provided without furniture or implements. Chief clerk Sanders mean to people; his wife and son employed in service. Home economics teacher useless and dishonest in reports to Washington.

testimony.witness_title: Committee member, Agua Caliente Band of Mission Indians, Palm Springs
testimony.hearing: Senate Committee on Indian Affairs hearing
testimony.subject: Palm Springs Indian land boundary issues, water rights, trading post, airport
testimony.key_claims: Old boundary lines lost; white neighbors continuously encroaching. Forefathers tilled soil and brought Tahquitz Canyon water for irrigation but agent McCallum drove them away. Cemetery still visible with fig trees as markers. Pedro Chino is last member of family after whom Chino Canyon was named. Water company organized in 1909 laid pipe line through Indian land sections 4, 5, 6, and 10; Mr. Rogers agreed to give small water portion for domestic use as intake was on their land, but agent Miss C. True refused. Agent Ellis gave no satisfaction. Tahquitz Canyon water dries up every summer, is unsafe, flows through open ditch. Five other landowners given water from ditch leaving Indians short. Have to pay water company for domestic water; some members had water shut off. Trading post at Palm Canyon established without consent. County constructed highway through Indian land without compensation. Airport taken with understanding tribe would receive money but never paid. Request to reestablish old boundaries with substantial monuments.

testimony.hearing: Senate Committee on Indian Affairs hearing
testimony.subject: Visits to Palm Springs reservation
testimony.key_claims: Has visited Palm Springs about seven times. Tribe visited his office less than a week ago as full committee. Received a pleasant letter after their visit stating they were pleased with what he said and would consider what he talked about.

testimony.hearing: Senate subcommittee hearing at Yuma Reservation
testimony.subject: Conditions of Yuma and Cocopah Indians
testimony.key_claims: Many Yuma Indians do not have money to provide proper clothing and food. Cocopahs exist under squalid conditions: little mud house, no sanitary arrangements, mud floors, no furniture. No reimbursable money to buy implements for Cocopahs trying to farm. They borrow implements and work animals from each other. Despite all this, stated the Yumas are in fairly satisfactory condition. Yumas preferred as workers over Mexicans but cannot get employment. Yumas denied agricultural credit and admittedly cannot farm their own lands without it.

testimony.hearing: Senate subcommittee hearing at Yuma Reservation
testimony.subject: Department investigation of Yuma Indian complaints
testimony.key_claims: Department was making an investigation of all the matters raised by the Yumas about their treatment. After 2 years in office, still making undesignated investigation.

testimony.witness_title: Committee Member, Agua Caliente Band of Mission Indians
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Grievances of Agua Caliente Band including land boundaries, water rights, airport compensation, trading post, and domestic water system
testimony.key_claims: White neighbors have been encroaching on tribal land; boundary lines are lost; water company refuses to grant water rights from Chino Canyon despite pipe running through Indian land; Tahquitz Canyon water is contaminated and shared with five non-Indian landowners leaving Indians short; airport revenues have not been paid to tribe; trading post established at Palm Canyon without consent; county built highway through reservation without consent; Superintendent Dady visited reservation only once since taking office (disputed by Dady); approximately $1,600-$1,700 in tribal fund but insufficient for water system; Indians willing to provide labor for water system at no cost

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Defense of his administration; water system project for Palm Springs; working conditions
testimony.key_claims: Has visited Palm Springs reservation approximately seven times, more than any other; manages 30 reservations, 20 of appreciable size, with 640 or more Indians and over 100 projects; works 12-15 hours per day; found $1,250.92 in airport lease funds; chamber of commerce paid additional $400; pipe alone costs $3,600, insufficient funds available; requesting $50,000 for miscellaneous irrigation work from Public Works; Indians can use their existing funds as they wish; asked Indians to suggest uses for funds; has confidence of Indians before outside agitators interfere; attorney for band confirmed Dady is treating them fairly

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Improper resurveying of Indian reservation boundaries; Los Coyotes boundary dispute with Warner Ranch; legal basis for Indian land rights
testimony.key_claims: Government sends eastern engineers who do resurveys instead of retracing original boundary lines; Indians cannot reconcile differences caused by resurveys; Los Coyotes Reservation has four official government surveys of same line, none findable on ground; Lightfoot 1910 resurvey shifted boundary nearly a quarter mile from original, dispossessing Indians of land and water they used before 1855; Indians have no maps or records of their land; General Land Office has no right to change boundaries of patented Indian lands; Indians entitled to compensation for land excluded by surveying mistakes per Choctaw Nation v. U.S.; Spanish law recognized Indian possessory rights; reservations in southern California given worthless, barren, mountainous land; recommends each reservation committee receive complete set of maps and field notes; Dady has confidence of Indians and understands their land problems

testimony.witness_title: Spokesman, Santa Ysabel Indian Reservation; Member, Mission Indian Federation
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Charges against Mission Indian Federation; opposition to Wheeler Bill; dissatisfaction with Commissioner Collier
testimony.key_claims: Commissioner Collier falsely charged Mission Indian Federation police with carrying guns; Special Agent Moore sent a telegram and refused to provide a copy when asked; Commissioner Collier has caused more dissension among Indians than any previous commissioner; Wheeler Bill would set Indians back 100 years by imposing tribal courts and customs; Mission Indians are voters and citizens who wish to continue on that basis; Indians of Santa Ysabel have no tribal customs; Collier stated at Muskogee conference that President Roosevelt personally appointed him

testimony.witness_title: California Indian community member and voter
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Complaints about Commissioner John Collier, the Wheeler Bill, employee retention under Dady, and conduct of Indian police
testimony.key_claims: Commissioner Collier has caused more dissension and dissatisfaction among Indians than any previous Commissioner; the Wheeler Bill was setting Indians back 100 years instead of advancing them; same employees remain from the Ellis era who mistreated Indians; Indian police are retained indefinitely without accountability; J. A. Moore sent a telegram to Collier about federation police carrying guns at Mesa Grande but would not show the telegram to Indians when asked; requested changes in the police force; stated he is a voter and citizen and wishes to continue as such; referenced Muskogee hearing page 20 where Collier stated he and Ickes were not appointed politically; stated Collier asked for Indian endorsement while his appointment was held up by Senator McAdoo

testimony.witness_title: Special Officer, United States Indian Service
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Mesa Grande fiesta incident of August 1933; telegram to Commissioner Collier; concealed weapons
testimony.key_claims: A telegram was sent about trouble at Mesa Grande fiesta; some federation police carried concealed weapons which he personally witnessed; Robert Magee was present at the fiesta but did not operate as an officer and was later discharged for inefficiency; no formal written charges had been preferred against John Lewis; Moore's authority comes from Washington and he has no connection to Mr. Dady
testimony.questioner: The Chairman; Senator Thomas; Mr. Couro

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Disputing Moore's claim that federation police were armed at Mesa Grande fiesta
testimony.key_claims: Moore is mistaken about federation police being armed; federation police are not allowed to carry any arms; Indians are peaceful people who do not need arms; Moore's report said several federation police were armed but he should name which ones; federation police carry nothing for protection, not even a club

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: John Lewis as Indian policeman; police force management
testimony.key_claims: John Lewis is as far as he knows a good policeman; Winslow is making a complaint against John Lewis; Mr. Moore is in charge of the police

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Disputing Moore's account of armed federation police at Mesa Grande fiesta August 5, 1933
testimony.key_claims: On the night of August 5, 1933, under Moore's leadership, no armed Indian Federation policemen were encountered; not one arrest was made; the fiesta went on very peacefully; Moore's report is not true; on many occasions Mission Indian Federation police were helpful rather than a disturbance
testimony.questioner: N/A (affidavit read into record by Mr. Couro)

testimony.witness_title: Deputy Special Officer at Large, United States Indian Service
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Mesa Grande fiesta incident August 1933; confrontation with federation Indians; Willis and Prather inciting resistance
testimony.key_claims: Moore testified that federation Indians challenged his authority at Mesa Grande fiesta, threatened violence, claimed only federation police had authority, and that Willis had urged Indians to resist government officers. He claimed Indians were armed. He described de-escalating a potentially violent confrontation and sending telegram to Collier for backing. He characterized Willis, Prather, and Collett as dangerous racketeers interfering with government work.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Mesa Grande incident; Los Coyotes resurvey; Mission Indian welfare
testimony.key_claims: Co-signed letters asserting Moore made false charges; Willis never advised resorting to violence; Federation police never carry arms or offered physical resistance; Anderson failed to properly retrace old survey lines; Indians were not incited by Willis or Castillo to sign away rights.

testimony.witness_title: Mission Indian advocate; Mission Indian Federation
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Mesa Grande incident; Los Coyotes resurvey; Indian Bureau conduct; Sycuan reservation espionage
testimony.key_claims: Moore made totally false charges manufactured out of whole cloth; no disturbance occurred while Willis was at fiesta on August 4, 1933; Willis left at 10:30 p.m. before alleged incidents; Willis's car was set on fire and Moore's police did nothing; Anderson attempted to fraudulently obtain Indian signature on land exchange paper; Dady and Anderson acted in concert against Indian interests; Indian policemen are cause of friction among Mission Indians; no Indian policemen are needed in southern California.

testimony.witness_title: Citizen, La Jolla; Mission Indian advocate
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.committee: Senate Indian Affairs Committee and House Indian Committee
testimony.subject: Mesa Grande fiesta account; Sycuan reservation gag rule and espionage; Moore's false accusations
testimony.key_claims: Prather and companions left Mesa Grande fiesta at 9 p.m. finding it entirely peaceful and orderly; school meeting was open and non-secret; Moore's telegram to Collier was maliciously conceived with neither truth nor basic fact; Frank Wachano attempted to prevent Prather from entering Sycuan reservation on orders from Riverside; Riverside office engaged in gag rule and espionage; Wachano was stool pigeon for superintendent.

testimony.witness_title: Local Superintendent, Mission Indian Agency, Riverside
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Armed Indians at Los Coyotes; Anderson survey commission
testimony.key_claims: Dady was not present at the Los Coyotes meeting but stated Rieger was there and would testify he saw Indians armed. Implied armed Indians were present.

testimony.witness_title: Chief of E.C.W., Mission Indian Agency under Dady
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Whether Indians were armed at Los Coyotes meeting
testimony.key_claims: Rieger stated he was not familiar with all men present but saw Nicholas Chaparosa had a gun in plain view that afternoon. Was uncertain about other men because he was not familiar with them at the time.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Whether Nicholas Chaparosa had a gun at the meeting
testimony.key_claims: La Chusa knew Nicholas Chaparosa and saw him that afternoon but stated he was not even a federation police, implying he did not have a gun in an official capacity; testimony appeared to contest Rieger's claim.

testimony.hearing: N/A - statement referenced in letter
testimony.committee: Senate Indian Affairs Committee (referenced in September 10, 1934 letter)
testimony.subject: Moore's accusations about armed Indians at Mesa Grande fiesta
testimony.key_claims: McGee stated that Moore's accusations against Indians carrying arms at Mesa Grande fiesta were false.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Reservation boundary survey dispute between Los Coyotes Indians and ranch company
testimony.key_claims: Anderson stated he returned Dady's commission because doing the work as Dady wanted would cause Indians to lose their lands. He offered to retrace old lines for free as Indians showed him, stating he was a licensed surveyor with much experience in land titles. He had completed a 100+ page survey of Soboba Reservation showing Indians justified in claiming ranch lands near San Jacinto. Stated the title company cannot give a good title free from Indian claims.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Alleged armed Indians at reservation
testimony.key_claims: Stated that one man, Nicholas Chaparosa, had a gun in plain view that afternoon. Was not familiar with all men present and could not say positively about others. Was a new employee at the time attempting to start the E.C.W. program.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Moore's presence on reservation during fiesta; Nicholas Chaparosa gun allegation; Indian police authority
testimony.key_claims: Stated Nicholas Chaparosa is not even a federation police and did not have a gun. Denied that 75 Indians gathered to chase Moore off reservation, saying Coonrod was present and they were discussing school matters. Stated they asked Moore who sent him and to show papers; he only showed a badge and a card. Two years ago other officers claimed to be U.S. marshals and showed nothing. Stated Indians told Moore Friday morning he could stay and they would let him know Saturday evening. Saturday told him they didn't need him but he could stay. Accused previous officers of shining lights on women going to toilet. Argued Indians should have voice in selecting Indian police.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Incident at Indian reservation fiesta; law enforcement authority; Indian police appointment
testimony.key_claims: Stated incident occurred around 10:30 or 11 at night with over 75 Indians present; they made every effort to remove him short of laying hands on him. Has been in service about 2 years covering California, Arizona, Nevada - about 50 reservations. Went to fiesta committee to identify himself and seek cooperation, offering to work with committeemen. Offer was flatly refused. Told he was not wanted. Committee later said they didn't want any officer interfering with anyone selling liquor. Told him to stay in fiesta grounds and not make arrests or he could not stay. One man arrested for bringing liquor onto reservation and giving it to Indians - this man was white. Read telegram from Commissioner Collier verifying his authority. Had arranged with Miss McGair and Superintendent Ellis that Indian police would be recommended by tribe first; Dave Navarro appointed on Santa Rosa Reservation following this procedure.

testimony.witness_title: Saboba Mission Indian, representative of Mission Indian Federation
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Reservation boundary lines, California Indians' Court of Claims case, attorney general representation, Indian police selection, Bureau of Indian Affairs conduct
testimony.key_claims: Represents many tribes in San Diego and Riverside Counties, approximately 2,500 in Mission Indian Federation. Government failed to show Indians true boundaries of reservations; Indians have lost corners and don't know what land belongs to them. Requests lines be retraced. Government authorized attorney general to file suit; Attorney General Webb filed for $12,800,000. Collier's magazine stated Indians would only get $6,000,000 which would be only $250-300 per person for 23,000 California Indians. Indians sent delegates to Washington spending $400-500. Indians want their own attorney; object to defendant hiring attorney for plaintiff. Attorney General has never consulted with Indians and Indians have no way to consult with him. Indians believe Attorney General wants to settle for $6,000,000. Indians want case handled in Court of Claims. Government Indian police are hand-picked by Indian agent without Indian voice; police say they work for Government not Indians. Mission Indian Federation engaged attorney Mr. Butler in Washington. Case involves Temecula and Santa Isabel treaties covering San Diego and Riverside Counties.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Attorney General Webb's cooperation with California Indians
testimony.key_claims: Speaking on behalf of Attorney General Webb: When Senator Wheeler wrote regarding the investigation, Webb sent for her and expressed his willingness and cooperation as far as Indians are concerned, and his anxiety to work for them in every possible way.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Character of Attorney General Webb
testimony.key_claims: Has been friend of California Indians for years. Knows Attorney General Webb and worked with him when anti-alien law was passed in California. Webb has been elected term after term for nearly 30 years. People of California have confidence in Webb. Vouches for Webb as honest man and able prosecutor.

testimony.witness_title: Indian advocate, close contact with Mission Indians
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Mission Indians' cooperation with new agent Dady; treaty case; fiesta incident; bureau employee misconduct
testimony.key_claims: Last July Mission Indians sent through Castillo a letter to newly appointed Dady offering whole-hearted cooperation. Willis introduced Dady to Indians who clapped in joy. Has shorthand notes of the meeting. Indians raised issues of treaties, Indian policemen/physical enslavement. Committee previously recommended removal of superintendent and transfer, also Miss McGair, also field agent at Campo where child starved to death; same bureau employees still in place. Agent did not wait to hear Indians' discussion of matters affecting them. Willis sent copy of endorsement letter to Collier who requested Indians' endorsement for President. Visited Attorney General with Mr. Ness; AG was interested but nothing accomplished; AG stated he would step aside if Indians could have their own attorney. After turndown by superintendent, Collier's magazine stated conflict in favor of Mission Indians would probably be $6,000,000, further inciting Indians.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Indian police appointment; his presence at reservation incident; E.C.W. program
testimony.key_claims: Was not present at reservation during the incident described. Rieger was there as new E.C.W. employee. Two Indian policemen appointed: one is spokesman of reservation; other was appointed by spokesman. Chief Myers is one appointee. Committed to carrying out plan of tribal recommendation for police appointments during his administration.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Identity as Indian policeman
testimony.key_claims: Confirmed he is an Indian policeman.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Indian policemen appointment; Mission Indians' cooperation letter to Dady; treaty matters; Attorney General situation; Court of Claims claim; fiesta conspiracy; Campo killings; ballot/election issues
testimony.key_claims: Testified that Mission Indians sent letter through Adam Castillo to new agent Dady offering cooperation; that agent refused to sit down with Indians; that treaties, Indian policemen, Indian hospital, and Indian voice in government were key concerns; that the estimated $6,000,000 Court of Claims conflict incited Indians; that there was no disturbance or drinking at the Indian fiesta; that there was a conspiracy by certain officials including Mr. Moore to have the wrong man confess to owning whisky at the fiesta; that the Campo killings seven years prior were committed by deputy sheriffs who exceeded authority entering reservation; that ballot for spokesman election required Indians to sign names making them 'marked Indians'; that same bureau employees remained despite prior committee recommendations for removal

testimony.witness_title: former executive secretary, Community Chest, San Diego
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Meeting at reservation where Purl Willis was making a speech to Indians
testimony.key_claims: Testified that he arrived at a reservation meeting expecting to meet captains; found Willis making a speech to Indians that he characterized as not beneficial or cooperative; that Willis changed tone upon seeing visitors arrive; that the meeting itself with Adam speaking was excellent; implied Willis was telling Indians they could get whatever they wanted

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Election of spokesmen; cooperation with Superintendent Dady; Campo school; loan inequality among Indians
testimony.key_claims: Stated Dady picked him as election judge without consulting him first, which caused Indians to go against Dady; requested written statement from Chairman confirming cooperation directive so he could show Government officials; said some Indians got loans for homes while others could not despite claim there was no money; said Campo School not being made available to Indians as community house; said if another election were held it would satisfy the people; demanded Dady confirm he would cooperate

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Spokesman elections; cooperation with Indians; house construction; relationship with Adam Castillo
testimony.key_claims: Stated the ballot issue had already been discussed before the House; said he called together four leaders including Tom Lukas and Winslow Couro to agree on election process; said he waited 6 weeks then called election December 28; said he had worked more with Adam than any other Indian; said a third election would not do any good as election was for one year; stated he asked for 200 new homes after C.W.A. homes were erected; said outside white interference was the main problem; confirmed willingness to cooperate with Adam Castillo

testimony.witness_title: attorney for Mission Indians of California
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Mission Indians' Court of Claims suit; role of California Attorney General; cooperation with government
testimony.key_claims: Stated he approved of committee's suggestion to take up suit with California attorney general; said he would use influence with Adam Castillo to encourage cooperation; told Indians when employed that he did not think the suit was being conducted to produce best results; said it was anomalous and unfortunate for a State officer to be named by Congress as attorney for Indians in a Federal matter; said nothing like it had happened before in government history

testimony.witness_title: resident of Capitan Grande Indian Reservation
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Relocation from Capitan Grande due to dam construction; request for government purchase of Viejas/Baron Long Ranch
testimony.key_claims: Government promised new place to live; identified Viejas or Baron Long Ranch as desired new location; petitioned government to buy it with money paid for water basin; dam nearly complete with 90-day relocation deadline; currently farming minimally with no stable home; road to new area is bad; two groups want to move together; believes it would be good place for Indians to live

testimony.witness_title: President, American Indian Defense Association of Northern California; attorney
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: California Indians claims bill; Court of Claims suit; role of Indian Defense Association
testimony.key_claims: Association had much to do with Commonwealth Club of California and Congressman Lee in framing H.R. 491 claims bill; helped put it through Congress; current Commissioner of Indian Affairs was in Congress actively engaged in getting bill through and was then executive secretary of Indian Defense Association; association is entirely a white organization; very interested in pending Court of Claims claim

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: Klamath Reservation matters (deferred to afternoon)
testimony.key_claims: Requested to testify in afternoon; expected another man with him who did not arrive

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: Lower Klamath River Indians' presence at hearing
testimony.key_claims: Present for two weeks; from the Lower Klamath River (distinct from Klamath Reservation Indians)

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.committee: Senate Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Complaints about Indian agent Mr. Dady and conditions on La Mesa Augustine Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Agent Mr. Dady has never visited La Mesa Augustine Reservation and does not know the troubles and hardships there. The agent has never helped Julian Augustine despite magazines claiming otherwise. Augustine requested investigators be sent to see conditions firsthand.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.committee: Senate Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Conditions on Cabazon Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Signatory to statement about conditions; details not specified beyond co-signing Augustine's statement

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.committee: Senate Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Conditions on Torro Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Signatory to statement about conditions; details not specified beyond co-signing Augustine's statement

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.committee: Senate Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Conditions on Martinez Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Signatory to statement about conditions; details not specified beyond co-signing Augustine's statement

testimony.witness_title: President, American Indian Defense Association of Northern California
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.committee: Senate Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: Role of American Indian Defense Association and California Indians claims bill
testimony.key_claims: Elkus stated he is president of the American Indian Defense Association of Northern California, a white organization. He stated the association cooperated with the Commonwealth Club of California and Congressman Lee in framing the California Indians claims bill and helping pass it through Congress. He noted the current Commissioner of Indian Affairs was formerly executive secretary of the Indian Defense Association and actively worked to pass the bill.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.committee: Senate Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: Klamath Reservation Indians
testimony.key_claims: Mitchell confirmed he was from Klamath Reservation; expected another man with him; requested to be heard in the afternoon

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.committee: Senate Subcommittee of the Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: Lower Klamath River Indians' presence and availability
testimony.key_claims: Stated they are from the Lower Klamath River and would be present for 2 weeks

testimony.hearing: Conference with Indian delegates
testimony.location: Office of Attorney General of California
testimony.subject: Role of attorneys in California Indians case
testimony.key_claims: Webb stated he was not familiar with the work involved and not prepared to choose attorneys; expected to employ an attorney to do hard labor; recommended against making chosen attorney a deputy; wanted attorneys to remain in private capacity working with their clients; stated he had known Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley for many years and congratulated Indians on their choice.
testimony.questioner: Indian delegates including 20 representatives, J. W. Henderson, J. B. Pemberton, James M. Hanley

testimony.hearing: Court of Claims hearing on attorney of record
testimony.subject: Authority of attorney general versus private attorneys in California Indians case
testimony.key_claims: Webb argued authority under which he proceeded was unusual; found nothing more applicable in cases and authorities than cases cited by counsel; felt it would be worthless to submit cases at all. Court authorized him to offer amendments; amended petition included all amendments previously proposed by friends of the court, including all Indians of California as claimants.

testimony.hearing: Conference with friends of the court regarding amendments
testimony.location: Office of Attorney General of California
testimony.subject: Proposed amendments to original petition, particularly inclusion of all Indians of California as claimants
testimony.key_claims: Webb declared he did not agree with amendment including all Indians of California 'at all, at all, at all'; stated there was nothing in the law or hearings to justify such assumption; opined act only authorized suit on behalf of Indians who negotiated treaties and their descendants. Friends of the court showed by hearings and the act itself that Webb's interpretation was in error; Webb did not admit or deny validity at conclusion.
testimony.questioner: Friends of the court (J. W. Henderson, J. E. Pemberton, James M. Hanley)

testimony.witness_title: Delegate, Indian Board of Cooperation; member of Requa Indian Auxiliary and board of directors
testimony.hearing: Affidavit in Court of Claims
testimony.subject: Representation of California Indians in Court of Claims case; desire for private attorneys; criticism of Attorney General Webb
testimony.key_claims: Indians of California are organized into more than 100 auxiliaries; Indians desire to be represented by Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley; attorney general took 15 months to file original petition which was inadequate; Webb failed to make amendments for over 2 years after errors were pointed out; retainer of $20,000 is less than $1 each for Indians of California; Indians never desired Webb to act for them; Indians are citizens of California and United States and have right to make own contracts.

testimony.witness_title: Delegate, Indian Board of Cooperation; member of Friant Indian Auxiliary and board of directors
testimony.hearing: Affidavit in Court of Claims
testimony.subject: Representation of California Indians in Court of Claims case; desire for private attorneys; criticism of Attorney General Webb
testimony.key_claims: Same as Peter Williams affidavit; co-deponent; Indians desire Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley as attorneys; Webb's petition was inadequate and he delayed amendments for over 2 years; undue delay cost Indians hundreds of thousands of dollars in lost interest; Indians lost confidence in Webb.

testimony.hearing: Conference with friends of the court
testimony.subject: Progress of government accounting for California Indians case
testimony.key_claims: Accounting Department was not responsible for long delay; during 15 months between May 18, 1928 and August 12, 1929, 13 other Indian cases were filed giving them preference; found method to advance California Indians case from November 1932 to February 1932; would not take a full year to prepare accounting as only specific appropriations involved.

testimony.hearing: Congressional committee hearing on jurisdictional bill
testimony.committee: House and Senate Committees on Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Proposed jurisdictional act for California Indians
testimony.key_claims: Indians of California have prima facie meritorious claim against the United States; the bill properly protects interests of Indians and Government; recommended favorable consideration by committees.

testimony.hearing: Statement submitted to Court of Claims
testimony.subject: Indians' desire to be represented by Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley; criticism of Attorney General Webb's handling of case
testimony.key_claims: Indians chose their own attorneys who have served them well; Webb took 15 months to file petition, which was defective; Webb failed to amend petition for over 2 years after errors pointed out; Indians do not want Webb; F.G. Collett is highly respected by Indians; retainer of $20,000 is less than $1 per Indian; Indians have constitutional right to employ own attorneys; Webb's delay cost Indians hundreds of thousands in lost interest

testimony.hearing: Statement submitted to Court of Claims
testimony.subject: Indians' desire to be represented by Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley; criticism of Attorney General Webb's handling of case
testimony.key_claims: Co-signatory with Peter Williams of statement; same claims as Williams regarding attorneys and Webb's dereliction

testimony.hearing: Senate Committee hearing on S. 3572
testimony.subject: Opposition to amendments to California Jurisdictional Act; characterization of Collett's solicitation activities
testimony.key_claims: Since 1920 Collett and associates have solicited California Indians collecting sums far greater than $5,000 stated by Collett; described as organized racket with carefully guarded misrepresentations; attorney general proceeded with due diligence; delays chargeable entirely to General Accounting Office; amount of recovery predetermined; additional attorneys cannot expedite or increase judgment; possible net award would amount to $13,063,832; no per capita payments to be made from judgment; proposed amendments would strengthen Collett organization's ability to extract money from Indians; unfavorable report made on H.R. 7095 on April 16, 1934

testimony.hearing: Senate Committee hearing on S. 3572 / written submission
testimony.subject: Analysis of Commissioner's reports; need for private attorneys for Indians of California
testimony.key_claims: Case about to be settled for $6,000,000; Commissioner doubled probable judgment amount in Senate report after Butler's testimony; Commissioner's first report did not allow any value for rights guaranteed in treaties, only $1.25 per acre for land; Indians need private attorneys to question book charges; possible recovery should be $49,000,000 per Commissioner's earlier statement when seeking appointment; conspiracy to settle case for $6,000,000 temporarily broken; attorney general has not questioned book charges against Indians; Indians not allowed to question correctness of acreage or charges; Mr. Butler does not hold approved contract with Mission Indians

testimony.hearing: Court of Claims hearing, March 14, 1932
testimony.subject: Opposition to recognition of Henderson, Pemberton, and Hanley as attorneys of record; conduct of Indians of California case
testimony.key_claims: Stated he conferred with departmental heads soon after passage of jurisdictional act concerning preparation of Indians' case; stated contract was entered into by Indian Board of Cooperation and handed to him by attorneys; stated Collett or attorneys did not cause amendment of petition; stated he would have nothing to do with anyone connected with F.G. Collett; read letter about dues collection to court; claimed amendments were evidence of his diligence and good faith; opposed recognition of Indians' special attorneys as attorneys of record

testimony.witness_title: unknown (likely attorney or California organization representative)
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Status of Court of Claims suit for California Indians; opposition to private attorneys for California Indians; history of Jurisdictional Act
testimony.key_claims: Suit is practically ready for hearing before Court of Claims; delays due to getting information from Government bureaus and taking turn among similar cases; recovery was contemplated at $6-10 million when bill was formulated; bill was purposely framed to have attorney general represent Indians to avoid competition among organizations and contingent fee claims; there is no controverted matter, mostly computation; land value was fixed at $1.25 per acre; per capita distribution is contrary to bill's intent; at time of bill passage there were three Indian associations in California (Collett's, Tibbitts', and Indian Defense Association); California itself has real interest in Indian rehabilitation; he was part of one of those organizations and did not want fight over attorneyship; no proposal for compromise of which he is aware

testimony.witness_title: Executive Representative, Indians of California, Inc.
testimony.hearing: Subcommittee hearing at St. Francis Hotel
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: California Indian claims; conduct of attorney general; history of jurisdictional act; activities of John Collier; character of various witnesses
testimony.key_claims: Stephen Knight was delegate for Indians of California in 1922 then switched to Indian Brotherhood and Kahn bill; John Collier gave Knight $250 to organize Indian Brotherhood; William Fuller also switched sides; F. G. Collett's indictment related to Rellimeo Film Syndicate had nothing to do with Indian affairs and was dismissed; attorney general has been damagingly derelict; attorney general filed suit 15 months late causing other cases to be filed ahead; attorney general's petition had multiple errors including failing to include many tribes; attorney general failed to amend petition for additional 2 years 7 months; amendments included new parties and new subject matter filed 10 months after jurisdiction expired; attorney general wrongfully relied on defendant to prepare plaintiff's case; Indians need private attorneys; Indians of California Inc. was regularly incorporated and recognized by California courts; financial reports will show Collett was without compensation for years and is owed over $10,000; Commissioner misled Congressional committees and sought predetermined settlement of $6 million

testimony.witness_title: Indian from Ukiah, California; representing Indian Brotherhood
testimony.hearing: Subcommittee hearing at St. Francis Hotel
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: California Indian representation and claims
testimony.key_claims: Provided erroneous information per F. G. Collett; opposed Indians of California Inc. position; background: was delegate for Indians of California in 1922, then persuaded to switch to Indian Brotherhood and Kahn bill with $250 from John Collier

testimony.hearing: Subcommittee hearing at St. Francis Hotel
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: California Indian representation and claims
testimony.key_claims: Described by Collett as a free lance not long continuing activity with any Indian organization; provided testimony at hearing

testimony.hearing: Subcommittee hearing at St. Francis Hotel
testimony.location: St. Francis Hotel, San Francisco, California
testimony.subject: Character of F. G. Collett
testimony.key_claims: Attempted to lead committee to believe executive representative of Indians of California was indicted for misuse of mail and not vindicated; characterized by Collett as vicious misrepresentation

testimony.witness_title: Representative of Indian Defense Association, Attorney
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.committee: Senate Committee on Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: California Indians Court of Claims case, attorney representation, per capita distribution, legal expenses collected from Indians
testimony.key_claims: Legal assistance budget was provided so Indians would have benefit of total recovery without cost. No contingent fee arrangement was made or needed. Lost lands were valued at $1.25 per acre. California Indians have no general tribal organization unlike Navajo or Pueblo Indians, with about 150 bands and approximately 22,000 Indians. Three Indian associations existed at time bill passed: one represented by Collett, one by Tibbitts in the South, and the Indian Defense Association. Per capita distribution would be a mistake; money should benefit all Indians through a commission with U.S. Government, State of California, and Indian representation. Indians have been propaganded to desire certain attorneys. Attorney general would resign if certain attorneys were joined with him. Large sums ($17,000-$30,000 annually) have been collected from California Indians for legal expenses since 1922-1924. The real legal basis for recovery is right of occupancy under Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, not lost unsigned treaties. Original Raker bill was based on treaty rights but recovery should be for all California Indians.

testimony.witness_title: Representative of California Indian Organization (approximately 17,000 members)
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.committee: Senate Committee on Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: History of Court of Claims bill, attorney general's handling of case, need for Indian attorneys, per capita payment, organizational finances
testimony.key_claims: Attorney general was authorized to bring suit at Collett's solicitation. Attorney general had not progressed with suit as rapidly or thoroughly as anticipated. Fifteen months passed before suit was filed without attorneys being advised or given opportunity to assist. Petition was filed in error, excluding many tribes and several thousand Indians; attorney general misunderstood who his clients were. Attorney general prayed for unnecessarily fixed sum, limiting court recovery. Amendments needed for 2 years and 7 months before being made, and when made were 10 months after 3-year jurisdictional period. Indians have inherent constitutional right to be represented by attorneys of their own choice. Collett not an attorney and has no contract to share in any recovery. Per capita payment is for current Congress to decide, not previous Congress. Original Court of Claims bill prepared by Collett and presented personally to Judge Raker and Senator Phelan in 1920. In September 1928 Indian delegates contracted with Henderson, Hanley, and Pemberton as their attorneys. Organization claims to represent about 17,000 of 23,000 California Indians. Organization books not yet audited due to lack of funds; no salary paid to Collett for several years. Counter proposal by Indian Defense Association for $49,500,000 outright appropriation was unsatisfactory. Bill failed in 1920 due to House congestion, failed under Secretary Fall, received pocket veto approximately 1926.

testimony.witness_title: Representative, Indian organization for California Indians
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: California Indians Court of Claims case, attorney representation, bill history, delay in proceedings
testimony.key_claims: Organization represents approximately 17,000 of 23,000 California Indians via membership roll. Indians contracted with attorneys Henderson, Hanley, and Pemberton. Case delay caused by filing suit 15 months after jurisdictional act, allowing 13 other cases to be filed ahead. Jurisdictional act should not be amended but an extension of time for filing amendments to suit should be made. John Collier's report to committee contains errors. No testimony has been taken, many valuable witnesses are now dead, others aged and feeble. Indians of California are the litigants not the State. Court of Claims law does not predetermine values of claims. Repeatedly visited attorney general's office without satisfactory progress. Indians should have attorneys of their own choice. Mr. Stormont was called in by Collier to oppose Indians having their own attorneys but said he knew nothing about the bill. Mr. Collett opposed Collier's California State investigation bill as it would have delayed Court of Claims bill passage.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Status of California Indians Court of Claims case, timeline, attorney representation, estimated recovery, State appropriation
testimony.key_claims: Enabling act passed approximately one year before Federal act of 1920. Suit filed within 15 months of Federal act; Congress allowed 36 months. Conference held in Washington with DOJ, Indian Office, accountants, and Controller after suit filed. No compromise of case ever suggested or possible given nature of case. Indians were misled about delay being caused by failure of their attorneys; delay actually due to federal accounting process. Amended complaint filed after 3-year period but Webb believes amendments are sustainable. Indian contracted attorneys admitted as friends of court; denied as attorneys of record. Original complaint estimated $12 million total recovery; government offsets to be deducted. Claims of $150 million recovery circulating among Indians are unfortunate exaggerations. State legislature appropriated $15,000 for suit expenses; approximately $14,000 remains. Webb would not work with attorneys selected by or associated with Mr. Collett. Webb declined to approve Indian attorney contracts due to lack of authority and character of contracts. Webb recommended either allowing Indians to select their own attorneys with complete control, or maintaining current arrangement. California treaty Indians occupied good productive lands, were moved to poorer lands after agents falsely represented unratified treaties were in force, never received payment for personal property stipulated in treaties.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: California Indian claims, status of Court of Claims suit, attorney selection, treaty lands
testimony.key_claims: Webb stated he asked legislature for $15,000 appropriation for suit expenses and $14,000 remains. He regretted delays and representations made to Indians about fabulous sums. He has no objection to attorneys selected by Indians or court with safeguards, while eliminating state responsibility. He described California treaty Indians as having been moved from productive lands to poorer ones without receiving any payment or personal property stipulated in contracts. Federal agents moved them after representing unratified treaties were in force. Webb counseled freely with employed attorneys including Hanley, found all reputable and experienced. He felt it unfortunate attorneys were associated with Mr. Collett. He stated he does not know what government offsets will be but estimates situation will not be similar to Blackfeet case.

testimony.witness_title: Attorney for Mission Indians of Southern California
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Jurisdictional act amendment, Indian attorney selection, acreage testimony, value of treaty benefits, set-offs
testimony.key_claims: Butler stated he represents 3,000 Mission Indians not connected with other organizations heard that day. Mission Indians called at his Washington office in March 1934 fearing a predetermined consent judgment of $6,000,000. He pointed to October 15, 1933 Office of Indian Affairs publication and April 16, 1934 Department report on H.R. 7095 predetermining $6,000,000 net recovery. He argued jurisdictional act is not broad enough to do justice to Indians - does not confer jurisdiction to determine value of lands in 18 treaties, limits value to $1.25/acre. He successfully recovered $3.5 million for Ute Indians over Department opposition by killing set-offs. He argued Indians are entitled to attorneys of own selection, that amended petition should be filed asking court to authorize testimony on acreage, value of personal property, and propriety of government set-offs and book credits. He stated he does not want Webb to withdraw but wants to cooperate. He argued Court of Claims is a congressional not constitutional court and has never rendered judgments against government that were too large. California Indians rank much higher than average North American Indians. Money appropriated for Indians often went to somebody else.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Indian right to select own attorneys
testimony.key_claims: Stated that Indians should have their own attorneys; it would be fairer and they would feel better. Had prior experience with test case relevant to Indian rights.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Enrollment omissions, petition coverage gaps, extension of enrollment period
testimony.key_claims: It took attorney general 46 months to ascertain who his clients were before filing amended petition including several thousand previously omitted Indians. Families still not included in current petition including families driven from lands into desert. Robinson, the only man from the reservation in San Quentin, and his family were left out. Suggested Congress extend enrollment time 6 more months. California Indians have suffered longer and more than any other Indians.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Right to employ own attorney, 3-year filing limit, financial losses from delay
testimony.key_claims: As citizen of California entitled to full privileges of employing own attorney. Many Indians not satisfied with how case has been handled. Court of Claims act provided only 3 years for claims prosecution. If judgment money had been deposited in Treasury drawing 4 percent interest they would be far ahead; delays causing significant financial loss. Indians spent money employing attorneys and handling organization work.

testimony.witness_title: Government official, Office of Indian Affairs
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Enrollment roll status, omitted families
testimony.key_claims: Attorney general has nothing to do with making the enrollment roll. Judge Raker who made the roll made every effort to include everyone. Families are being found who were not reached and are being taken up, but time for accepting enrollment applications has elapsed. Final roll was completed and approved by Secretary as provided in law; no way applications may now be received.

testimony.witness_title: Attorney under contract with California Indians since 1928
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Indian desire for own attorneys, set-offs, attorney contract
testimony.key_claims: Has traveled the state meeting Indians in groups of 100 and 200 since appointed attorney. Consensus is almost unanimous - Indians want attorneys of their own choice. Compared situation to not wanting the opposing party to appoint your attorney. This feeling is not propaganda - Indians are intelligent and know what white people do with attorneys. Government took all this time to investigate set-offs so plaintiffs deserve reasonable time to independently investigate government set-off statements. Any citizen entitled to have an attorney in whom they have confidence and to change that opinion. If Indians desire to change attorneys under contract since 1928, he will facilitate that change. Known Webb for 30 years and practiced law with him. Indian Board of Cooperation had nothing to do with attorney contract; Indians themselves presented contract to Webb. Official statement furnished to committee that gross judgment and set-offs were predetermined should not have been accepted by attorney general as basis for petition for judgment. California Indians will never receive one-half or even one-third of what is due them unless proper testimony is taken.

testimony.witness_title: Attorney for California Indians, President of Indian Board of Cooperation
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Representation of California Indians in Court of Claims case, attorney contract, right of Indians to choose own attorneys
testimony.key_claims: Henderson stated he has been under contract with California Indians since 1928; traveled all over California meeting Indians in groups of 100-200; Indians unanimously want attorneys of their own choice; Attorney General should not be the one to appoint the opposing party's attorney; Indians were literally robbed in early days; he organized Indian Board of Cooperation in 1912 and secured 15 schools; he did not solicit the case; suggested amendments to attorney general who eventually incorporated all of them; believes petition is sufficient without amendment to act; testimony should have been taken long ago; attorney general is wrong to refuse association with chosen attorneys simply due to conflict with Collett; Collett has invaluable knowledge that should be utilized; damages including loss of medical care and education should be calculated even if difficult

testimony.witness_title: Attorney, practicing law in San Francisco since 1897
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Attorney contract with California Indians, representation of 17,000 Indians, Court of Claims case, attorney fees, jurisdictional amendment
testimony.key_claims: Hanley was invited to join by Henderson in 1928; contract signed after 1928 convention of Indian delegates representing 32 districts; visited Attorney General Webb with 24-26 delegates and explained everything in shorthand; Webb made no appointment and delayed filing petition and amendments; hearing concerns two issues: neglect to file jurisdictional amendment and whether Indian-chosen attorneys should continue; contract provides 2 percent on first $2 million and 3 percent on all over that; attorneys have traveled extensively throughout California; engaged Washington D.C. firm Esch, Kerr, Wooley, Taylor & Shipe on same proportional basis; attended meetings in Eureka with couple hundred Indians; contract not submitted to or approved by Indian Office; willing to accept quantum meruit contract if necessary; spent four solid months personally on case plus travel; Henderson made four trips to Washington; damages for loss of promised doctors and nurses should be presented to court; the act provides for just compensation which includes all elements of damage

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Opposition to private attorneys, accuracy of 17,000 Indian enrollment claim, sufficiency of Attorney General's representation
testimony.key_claims: Attorneys claiming to represent 17,000 Indians are exaggerating; 5,000 would be an exaggeration; enrollment has been ongoing for 20 years and Indians signing up do not know what it means, told they will get money; should have a showdown requiring attorneys to show how many adult Indians (21 and over) belong to the organization; old Indians who could testify about treaties do not exist as treaties were made 80 years ago and any surviving Indians would have been too young; survey of reservations would be expensive and charged against the bill; no opposition to the bill so private attorneys are unnecessary and wasteful; every little group would get a local attorney who might pay group leaders for access; private attorneys merely delay the case and add expense; Attorney General and his staff are sufficient representation

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Opposition to private attorneys representing California Indians; challenge to Indian Board of Cooperation membership claims
testimony.key_claims: Ainsworth argued that attorneys claiming to represent 17,000 California Indians were exaggerating, that 5,000 would be an overestimate. He alleged attorneys enrolled Indians by telling them they would get money, inducing families to sign up without understanding. He argued that old Indians who knew about the 1851-1852 treaties were no longer living or would have been too young to remember. He said surveys of reservations would add expense to the bill. He contended that the Attorney General was sufficient representation and that hiring private attorneys was unnecessary expense and delay, alleging attorneys bribed Indian group leaders with $200-$300 to secure contracts. He believed the bill would pass without opposition.

testimony.witness_title: Half-Indian, Chonschasi tribe (mother's side), collector for Indian Board of Cooperation
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Support for Indian Board of Cooperation and its attorneys; valuation of Indian land claims
testimony.key_claims: Walker defended the Indian Board of Cooperation, stating that Collett, Henderson, and Pemberton were the best friends California Indians ever had, having worked 20 years for the cause. He argued that without the organization's fundraising, no one would have funded the Indians' cause, citing 50 years of inaction by Government officials. He attempted to present the valuation of treaty tract lands including a 25-mile-square tract in Amador County with 13 gold mines including the Argonaut Mine, from which $262,000,000 was extracted around 1925. He argued the tract was worth over $100,000,000 even at the time of the treaties. He stated he collected approximately $2,000 from Indians and received only expense reimbursement for 4 years of work. He contended Indians would be lost without their chosen attorneys.

testimony.witness_title: Washoe Indian, Susanville; Auxiliary Chairman, Susanville Auxiliary
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Support for Mr. Collett and Indian Board of Cooperation
testimony.key_claims: Barrington stated that as auxiliary chairman representing 80 members in Susanville, the Indians in his district felt that Mr. Collett had done more for the Indians than any white man in the State. He challenged anyone to produce a white man better thought of than Collett through the mountain counties. He reported that 90 percent of Indians in his district were members of Indians of California, Inc. (new name for Indian Board of Cooperation) and urged him to come place that on record substantiating Collett's testimony.

testimony.witness_title: Indian, Ukiah, Mendocino County, Ukiah/Pomo tribe; founder of California Indian Brotherhood
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Opposition to Indian Board of Cooperation attorneys; challenge to membership claims; support for Attorney General Webb; presentation of documents showing propaganda against attorney general
testimony.key_claims: Knight stated he was formerly connected with the Indian Board of Cooperation but became discontented with money collection practices and misleading propaganda. He traveled to Washington with 7-8 delegates and worked 4 months on the court of claims bill, concluding that having a white man as organizational head collecting money from Indians made it impossible to get the bill through Congress. He and colleagues then organized the California Indian Brotherhood with no white men, estimated 3,000-5,000 active members plus nonactive members, representing Indians from various counties including all Hoopa Reservation and all Pit River Indians of Modoc County (approximately 800). He stated the Indian Board of Cooperation's 17,000 membership claim was false, as the roll was made years ago, many members have died, and younger generation is not involved. He claimed almost half of northern California Indians were satisfied with Attorney General Webb's handling of the suit and bitterly opposed to Collett's attorneys. He offered to submit letters from Indian Board of Cooperation (including originals signed by Collett and Fisher) and letters from Indians opposing the private attorneys to the committee.

testimony.witness_title: National Executive Secretary, Indian Defense Association
testimony.hearing: House Committee on Indian Affairs hearings
testimony.subject: Opposition to Indian Office reservation courts bill; California Indian legislation
testimony.key_claims: Strongly opposed passage of bill introduced by Commissioner of Indian Affairs to legalize reservation courts appointed by and under control of the superintendent or agent. Collaborated with C. Hart Merriam on H.R. 9497 as preferred alternative.

testimony.hearing: House Committee on Indian Affairs hearings
testimony.subject: Opposition to Indian Office reservation courts bill; California Indian legislation
testimony.key_claims: Strongly opposed passage of bill introduced by Commissioner of Indian Affairs to legalize reservation courts. Advocated for H.R. 9497 as vastly better alternative, noting it would avoid delay likely from Court of Claims bill and place fund disposition in hands of joint government-Governor commission.

testimony.hearing: House Committee on Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: H.R. 9497 and adverse report from Secretary of Interior
testimony.key_claims: Stated that in face of adverse report rendered by Secretary of Interior on her bill, it would be absurd to take up committee time trying to induce them to report it favorably.

testimony.hearing: Congressional floor discussion
testimony.subject: Indian Board of Cooperation solicitation of funds and California Indian situation
testimony.key_claims: Confirmed Cramton's statement of facts about Indian Board of Cooperation letter; stated he protested against publication and insisted on informing Indians they had been misinformed; stated efforts to secure direct appropriation were hopeless; stated that Indian Board of Cooperation was not represented at hearings on California Court of Claims bill; stated lack of cooperation by California Indians made difficult situation more difficult.

testimony.hearing: Congressional floor discussion
testimony.subject: Indian Board of Cooperation solicitation of funds from Indians
testimony.key_claims: Placed in record lengthy communication signed by J.W. Henderson for Indian Board of Cooperation appealing for moneys from Indians; stated communication dated June 1 asked for money to promote passage of Court of Claims bill although it had already become law; stated F.G. Collett was under indictment for using mails to defraud and a new indictment might well have followed the above attempt.

testimony.hearing: Congressional floor discussion
testimony.subject: Indian Board of Cooperation's role in passage of California Court of Claims bill
testimony.key_claims: Stated that when Congressman Lea had his bill before the Committee on Indian Affairs, Collett and his organization had no influence whatever in the hearings and took no part in the passage of the bill.

testimony.witness_title: Chief of Mewuk Tribe of California
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Contract with Indian Board of Cooperation attorneys; criticism of Collett's leadership; withdrawal from Board of Cooperation
testimony.key_claims: Fuller stated that delegates who signed contracts should be held responsible for those contracts and pay pro rata of what they receive from the Federal Government. He claimed he always submitted affairs to his Indian people before acting. He criticized how delegates claimed to represent the whole State without proper authorization. He said Collett misled people and that his tribe viewed Collett as a reverend-like figure who misled them. His tribe retired from the Board of Cooperation when they found Collett was misleading them. Fuller also stated in his prior letter that the attorney for Indian Board of Cooperation represents not more than seven or eight tribes, not a majority, and that the contract was made by a vast minority without knowledge or consent of the majority.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Collections by Collett; role of Indian Board of Cooperation in passage of H.R. 491
testimony.key_claims: Submitted documents showing Collett collected $10,000 or more in 1923 and $11,000 in 1924. Contradicted Collett's claim that his organization was responsible for passage of H.R. 491, noting Collett was indicted February 14, 1928 and not apprehended until August 14, 1928, so was not present during March 8 and March 17 hearings. Submitted testimony of Levitt and Lee from December 11, 1928, stating Collett's organization was not present at hearings and played no part in passage of the bill. Stated her organization does not collect money from Indians.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Support for Collett and attorneys hired by Klamath Indians
testimony.key_claims: Stated that the Klamath Indians wanted Collett and his lawyers, hired them, and she knows what money was collected. Defended them as true Indian friends and said Indians should not undermine them for their own cause.

testimony.witness_title: Unknown, member of Owens Valley community
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Owens Valley Indians' water and land loss; right to choose own attorneys
testimony.key_claims: Stated that the city of Los Angeles took the water away from Owens Valley and people are destitute. Asserted that Owens Valley people were overlooked by Webb and therefore needed to hire their own attorney. Claimed that Indians used to own the whole valley but white people took it. Acknowledged some people sold land for whatever they could get. Defended Indians' right to choose their own attorneys and to spend their money on their organization. Expressed belief that the bill (H.R. 491/Court of Claims suit) was the result of their organization and contributions.

testimony.witness_title: State Chairman of Indian Citizenship, California State Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: DAR activities for California Indians; opposition to Collett and private attorneys; observations at Indian Board of Cooperation meetings
testimony.key_claims: DAR has ~5,000 members in ~80 chapters, each with Indian chairman. DAR policy is to help Indians become good citizens on equal footing with whites.
