DAR spent $755.77 in cash plus donations of clothes, building materials, furniture, medicine, books that past year. DAR provides student loan fund, supports helpful legislation, assists aged Indians in securing aid. DAR opposes stirring up dissatisfaction among Indians or inciting hatred of government. Arranged tuberculosis clinics in Tuolumne, Placer, Mendocino Counties; Dr. Mildred E. Thoren donated services; over 100 Indians examined. Attended Indian Board of Cooperation meetings at Nashville, El Dorado County. At first meeting, Collett and Hanley speeches designed to stir up dissatisfaction with State's handling of Court of Claims case and repeatedly urged Indians to contribute to private attorney fees (Henderson, Pemberton, Hanley; fee $20,000). At April 5, 1931 meeting Collett stated $100-500 million would be asked in petition; said suit ready for trial 'last fall' (1930) per attorney Schype of Washington D.C. firm; criticized Webb's conduct. At May 24, 1931 meeting Lipps and Judge Baker of Indian Office were present. Concluded that Collett should not collect money from destitute Indians who need county/state/federal aid. Opposed Dockweiler bill on grounds private attorneys do not represent all California Indians. Observed considerable cash paid at secretary's table after meetings.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Nature of the Court of Claims suit as a matter between California Indians and the Government
testimony.key_claims: Stated that the suit is a suit between the California Indians and the Government. Her auxiliary has about 50 or 60 members.

testimony.witness_title: Member of Daughters of the American Revolution
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Activities of California Indians Inc. and Frederick O. Collett collecting attorney fees from destitute Indians
testimony.key_claims: Attended meetings in Nashville El Dorado County in 1930 and April 5 1931 and May 24 1931. Collett and Hanley made speeches designed to stir dissatisfaction with State handling of Court of Claims case. Collett stated 100 million to 500 million dollars would be sought. Attorney fee set at $20,000. Collett said suit was ready for trial in fall of 1930 but also said Indians not ready until money collected. Cash collected at secretary's table after meetings. Indians are destitute and being asked to contribute to attorney fees while seeking county state and federal aid. DAR organization constantly appealed to by same Indians for assistance.

testimony.witness_title: Member of Kiteemu Tribe, Molelumne; auxiliary member of California Indians Inc.
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Defense of California Indians Inc. and the hiring of private attorneys; conditions of Kiteemu tribal members
testimony.key_claims: Auxiliary comprises about 50-60 members. Members voluntarily contributed dues and selected their own attorneys freely. Attorneys are sincere friends who did not initially ask for pay. Doubted Attorney General Webb would represent Indians' interests as fully as private attorneys. Tribal land is of poorest class, steep rocky hillsides. Son had been bedridden for 2 years with heart trouble from high school injury. Family received no outside help. Indians need a just settlement including land with water. Criticized DAR witness for neglecting Molelumne.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Sacramento Indian Agency's approach to California Indian conditions and attorney fee collection controversy
testimony.key_claims: Agency covers 40 counties of central and northern California. Has taken no part in attorney controversy. Believes Indians should have equal rights with all citizens. Main problem is getting Indians to concentrate on development rather than agitation. Has demonstrated California Indians have ability. Receives many letters complaining about methods of collecting funds from poor Indians. Trying to bring in county welfare, agricultural extension, state educational department and local agencies to help California Indians. Wants factionalism and agitation suppressed. Has shown that Indians given farms and education will make fine citizens.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Klamath Indian Reservation misadministration by Superintendent Wade Crawford and violations of Public Act 435
testimony.key_claims: Current superintendent Wade Crawford is unqualified to administer tribal business worth $30,000,000. Klamath Indians have repeatedly appealed to Commissioner without reply. Two sales of timber made on Klamath in violation of Public Act 435 without consent of general council. Commissioner admitted violation to Senator Steiwer but refused to act further. Affidavits document people jailed for standing up for rights, pregnant woman handled roughly and jailed without matron causing baby's death, and loose business methods. Came to hearing at own personal expense after superintendent refused to pay travel expenses. Situation nearly broke into open warfare. Requested proper investigation of Klamath situation.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Klamath timber sales violations, grazing irregularities, and Crawford's administration
testimony.key_claims: Numerous irregularities on reservation. Klamath Indians virtually unanimous against Crawford as superintendent. Have appealed to Commissioner repeatedly for removal or transfer with no reply. Harold Weaver's report shows approximately one million feet sold to Land Lumber Co. at $5-$5.50 per thousand with about 50 percent beetle infected. One million feet sold to Crane Lumber Co. from Bly Ridge at $4.50 per thousand with about 45 percent beetle infested. Zimmerman letter to Senator Steiwer stated less than 25 percent merchantable timber. Violation is selling without consent of general council per Act 435. Crawford removed sheep 3 years ago then brought them back through relatives on conditional sales contracts. Under treaty rights 500 head per family member free but family members sold to each other to circumvent limits. Crawford allowed Crystal to bring sheep onto reservation before surplus range was advertised for bidding.

testimony.witness_title: Foreman of beetle-control logging operation, Klamath Indian Reservation
testimony.hearing: Submitted as affidavit to Senate committee record
testimony.subject: Logging operations in Beetle Control Camp on Klamath Indian Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Logging on Bly Ridge was poor beetle-control measure. Instructed by forester Howarth and Superintendent Crawford to cut logs not less than 24 inches at stump down to 12-inch top and take all spike tops. Most spike-top trees taken were not beetle infested. Bug-infested trees smaller than cutting specifications were left standing. Crane Co. contracted for logs delivered at roads. Logs were to be scaled after Crane hauled them to mill rather than at roadside. Same issues applied at Skellog Draw. Only cream of timber was logged. Methods used differed from other beetle-control camps. No brush was piled or bug-infested butts treated that were left.

testimony.hearing: Submitted as affidavit to Senate committee record
testimony.subject: Wade Crawford's denial of assistance during husband George Gallagher's fatal illness
testimony.key_claims: In June 1933 husband asked Crawford for permission to sell four steers purchased with children's money to fund needed operation; Crawford refused unless money immediately returned to children's account. Later when husband was bedfast Crawford refused to give any of children's money or allow steers to be sold. Crawford told her to go get a job herself. Only received two purchase orders for food and clothing for children approximately 2 months before husband's death. About 3 weeks before death Crawford's brother-in-law Ted Savage posed as cattle buyer twice trying to purchase the four steers. About a week before death Crawford sent Indian Officer Arkell and Deputy Sheriff Fluey to move husband to hospital; refused on doctor's orders due to husband's extremely low vitality. Dr. Soule and Inez personally believe operation at time first requested would have saved George Gallagher's life.

testimony.hearing: Submitted as affidavit to Senate committee record
testimony.subject: Arrest and jailing while pregnant on Crawford's orders in January 1934
testimony.key_claims: In first week of January 1934 while pregnant went to Klamath Indian Agency to request money for groceries and clothing. Mr. Wilson refused. Crawford called her back and gave $20 purchase order. Crawford then wanted to know why she would not go to a home for wayward girls as he had previously tried to arrange. She refused stating she was of age. Crawford came outside and took keys of automobile. When she returned inside Henry Shadley Indian officer told her Wade said to take her. She refused to get in his car so Shadley grasped her around stomach and threw her into car knowing she was visibly pregnant. Brought to Chiloquin then returned to agency for Arkell to consult then returned to Chiloquin jail at 2pm. No fire in jail, very little and very dirty bedding, kept overnight without fire or food. Given breakfast at 10 next morning. Aunt refused permission to stay with her. No matron in attendance. Kept in large room with all other prisoners. Released about noon following day and was very ill. Baby born about a month later on February 4 1934, lived 2 days and died. Dr. Soule informed her the treatment greatly endangered health and lives of both baby and herself.

testimony.hearing: Submitted as affidavit to Senate committee record
testimony.subject: Arrest and jailing following confrontation with Crawford at December 27 1933 business committee meeting
testimony.key_claims: Attended open meeting of Klamath business committee on December 27 1933 to vote on expenses of delegates to Washington. Mrs. Wade Crawford arose to protest eligibility of one delegate. When member raised point of order Crawford began to vilify delegate with obscene names. Lang arose to ask chairman if meeting was meant to hear quarrels. Crawford swore at her told her to shut her mouth and advanced toward her with clenched fists in threatening manner and said he would throw her out. Several men intervened to prevent him striking her. Deputy Indian officer asked her to sit down. Henry Shadley arrived after Crawford telephoned him and placed her under arrest. Brought to Federal jail at Chiloquin about 3pm and kept overnight. Released next day.

testimony.witness_title: Klamath Indian allotment owner on Chiloquin Ridge
testimony.hearing: Submitted as affidavit to Senate committee record
testimony.subject: Unauthorized sheep grazing on Chiloquin Ridge and Crawford withholding reimbursable money
testimony.key_claims: First affidavit: On approximately April 1934 inspected allotment on Chiloquin Ridge and saw about 2000 sheep grazing under charge of Mr. Crystal husband of Cora Miller sister-in-law of Crawford. Sheep had been there about 10 days. Crystal said given permission by Crawford and Philipps stockman. Prior to this general council passed resolution requiring surplus range leased to highest bidder. Chiloquin Ridge classified as surplus range. Bids submitted April 27 1934 then turned over to business committee in June 1934. Second affidavit: Has small place on allotment not leased to sheepmen where he runs 5-6 hogs. Went to agency with son to get reimbursable money for buck rakes and harness. After consulting Crawford or Wilson agency informed son could not get reimbursable money despite having money in account. Crawford was holding son's per capita check and refused to release account money or reimbursable money until hogs were moved from Chiloquin Ridge.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Beetle-control logging and grazing rights abuses at Klamath Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Zimmerman's letter to Senator Steiwer stated less than 25% merchantable timber with rest bug-infested; trees marked for cutting were left standing; timber sold too cheaply. General council adopted resolution to sell grazing rights to highest bidder but Crawford allowed Crystal to bring sheep onto reservation before ranches were advertised for bid. Crawford was instrumental in removing sheep and then returning them under guise of Indian ownership through conditional-sales contracts with sisters-in-law and wife's nephew. Engle sold 500 head of sheep each to mother and sister without right to do so. Kirk requests thorough investigation into violation of Act 435 and asks committee to request Weaver's report on beetle-control logging.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States
testimony.subject: Appeals to Commissioner of Indian Affairs
testimony.key_claims: Tribe has appealed to Commissioner in person and in writing and in every way possible without satisfactory response.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in United States (written statement)
testimony.subject: Indian Court of Claims bill and legal representation dispute
testimony.key_claims: In 1922 F.G. Collett threatened Indians who did not subscribe to Indian Board of Cooperation would be left off rolls. In 1925 Tuolumne auxiliary held joint meeting with Eureka Indians; Collett failed to answer questions about funds and statements; auxiliary discontinued relations with board. Claims that 17,000 Indians voted to hire Henderson Pemberton & Hanley is in error because Me-wuk section of Calaveras, Tuolumne, and parts of Mariposa Counties had no voice or representative at those meetings. Me-wuk Tribe flatly refuses to accept Henderson Pemberton & Hanley as representatives. Tribe supports Attorney General U.S. Webb and will contest any fee allowed to the rejected law firm.
